name: Rack-and-pinion lengthening device

card.summary: A mechanically driven internal lengthening rod in which a twisting motion separates the bone in small steps, used in limb lengthening surgery to add height.
card.note: Limb lengthening is major surgery with reported complications including infection, additional operations and less gain than expected.

quick.overview:
A rack-and-pinion lengthening device is a type of lengthening implant in which a rod inside or alongside the bone is extended by a gear mechanism. Twisting the rod makes the gears push the two bone segments apart in small, set increments. The extra bone length that fills the gap is what produces added height, making it one of the mechanisms behind limb lengthening surgery.

Descriptions of limb lengthening note that manually operated devices of this kind separate the bone about a millimetre a day, usually in two steps, while the body grows new bone in the gap. Motorized and magnetic nails are alternatives that do the same job without manual twisting.
quick.how: In general terms, the surgeon cuts the bone and fits the device; after a rest period the bone is separated in small daily steps by twisting the rod, and the new bone then consolidates. The total length gained depends on the bone, the device and the surgeon. Patients then go through physiotherapy while the bone hardens.
quick.risks: Reported problems with limb lengthening in general include infection, additional surgeries, less height gained than expected and, in unregulated settings, patients being misled about risks. China's Ministry of Health banned the procedure in 2006 after a series of operations caused serious side effects. This is major orthopaedic surgery and is performed by specialist surgeons.

lead: A rack-and-pinion lengthening device is a mechanically adjustable implant used in limb lengthening (distraction osteogenesis) to separate a cut bone gradually. In the form described in general surveys of limb lengthening, the device is operated by twisting a rod that pushes the bone ends apart, with the separation done in set steps, typically about a millimetre per day in two steps [1].

For looks, the relevance is height: as the gap between the bone segments fills with new bone, the limb becomes longer and the person stands taller. In looksmaxxing discussions, the device type is one of several mechanisms people compare when researching cosmetic leg lengthening, alongside motorized nails such as the Fitbone and magnetic nails.

Surveys of the field also describe spring-based and motorized alternatives, and note that shape-memory alloys, springs and motors were being explored as ways to separate bone without manual intervention [1].

chain: Twisting motion drives a gear that extends a rod

New bone fills the gap and the limb lengthens
angle.text: The device is the mechanism that carries out the gradual bone separation in limb lengthening, so the height gained is permanent once the new bone has consolidated. The amount depends on the bone treated, the surgical plan and the device.

paras: In a rack-and-pinion arrangement, a toothed bar (the rack) is moved along its length by a small rotating gear (the pinion), converting rotation into straight-line movement. Applied to bone lengthening, the idea is that a rotating motion at the limb is converted into controlled linear extension of the implant. Surveys of limb lengthening describe manual devices of this kind as operated by twisting a rod that separates the bone [1].
The separation is carried out in set steps, typically around a millimetre per day split into two adjustments [1]. This pace is designed to let new bone form in the widening gap.

Motorized implants such as the Fitbone are described as fully implantable, with accurate deformity correction, low scar tissue formation and reduced infection risk, and patients are reported to find them more comfortable than mechanical systems [1]. Some devices apply continuous tension through a spring rather than discrete adjustments [1].

Cosmetic limb lengthening has been in demand in India, where it is described as unregulated; some patients were as young as 13 or 14, and reported problems include infections, additional surgeries, less height gained than expected and surgeons misleading patients about risks [1]. China's Ministry of Health banned limb lengthening in 2006 after a series of operations caused serious side effects [1].
No studies found specific to a rack-and-pinion device. Limb lengthening as a category is described in the orthopaedic literature and in general overviews [1].
